narrative:
The model predicted a 70.6% chance that you would fail the bar exam on your first attempt. Because this probability is well above the acceptance threshold, your law school application was rejected.

The decision was driven primarily by three factors from your academic record. Your first-year and third-year class rankings were the strongest influences, both pushing the prediction strongly toward failure. You placed in the bottom decile in both years, far below the average of roughly sixth decile among students who were accepted. These unusually low rankings signaled to the model that you would likely struggle with the demands of law school and the bar exam.

Your undergraduate GPA was the third most important factor, but it worked mildly in your favor. At 3.10 it sits only slightly below the 3.23 average of accepted students, giving the model a small reason to expect you might still pass.

Other details such as your LSAT score of 29 (versus an accepted average of 37), lower-middle family income, and full-time study plans played smaller roles and were not decisive. Gender and race were not used by the model at all.

To improve your chances, focus on raising your academic performance and retaking the LSAT to reach at least the mid-30s. Stronger grades and test scores in a future application would directly counteract the factors that led to this rejection.
